featured.content: Audio Transcript Welcome back to the podcast on this Thanksgiving week. Yesterday, we read about Jesus washing the feet of his disciples in John 13. Jesus worked his basin of water from disciple to disciple on the floor. When he reached Peter, Peter instinctively pulled his feet back and said, “You shall never wash my feet.” Then “Jesus answered him, ‘If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.’ Simon Peter said to him, ‘Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!’” Dump the basin on my head. Give me a shower! And then “Jesus said to him, ‘The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean’” (John 13:8–10). Peter is clean. He was chosen, and he was redeemed. Christ’s future work has already applied to him. Now he only needs his feet washed. Confessing sin is a part of daily cleansing (1 John 1:9), and that practice is never inconsistent with being “completely clean.” Peter is a living metaphor for justification and sanctification. And it tells me we can miss what Christ has done for us because we have dirt on our feet. We fixate on washing off the dust every day. We obsess over daily sanctification and forget that Christ washed us clean. Today on Ask Pastor John: how to beat scrupulosity. Today’s question is from a middle-aged man named Dave. “Pastor John, thank you for taking my question. I have struggled for many years with scrupulosity. That’s the word I learned last week while watching YouTube videos. When I looked up that word, scrupulosity, I wept for joy. My obsessive fears have destroyed my peace for many years. And I think I have discovered the root of most of my spiritual challenges and struggle with anxiety. So, now I want to ask you, Pastor John, what advice would you give to a man who has for years been paralyzed by scrupulosity?” There is a similarity between ordinary spiritual attacks that every believer endures, on the one hand, and more sustained obsessions that some believers endure, on the other hand. There’s a similarity. There’s an overlap. In other words, I don’t think we should overstate or understate the peculiar seriousness of what it is to deal with scrupulosity, or what is sometimes called obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Let me try to illustrate what I mean by the overlap between (1) the normal threat of a thought or an image or a behavior becoming an obsession that all of us experience and (2) the more persistent thoughts or images or behaviors that keep returning and returning, and won’t let a person have any rest, like a tick that bites you on the leg and sinks into your skin, and you try to pull it off, but it just grabs on deeper and harder. All of us deal with this danger. I’ve dealt with it personally and written about it, mostly in relation to sexual threats. For example, you inadvertently see some sexually riveting situation — say, a couple having sex on the ground behind your garage. Immediately, that image lodges itself in your consciousness with tremendous force. It threatens to take over. It wants to stay there and be developed in living color by your imagination. You can adapt this situation, this sexual temptation, to whatever your temptation is, whatever the threat of repetition is. You know the kind of thing I’m talking about. What do you do? Here’s my strategy. I’ll just sum it up quickly and then show how it might apply to this issue of scrupulosity. ANTHEM is my technique for handling a situation of threatening preoccupation with thoughts that ought not to be in my head. A: Avoid what triggers the thought or the image. If it’s inadvertent, don’t look back. If you can avoid the trigger in the first place, avoid it. N: Say no out loud to Satan, to your own mind. No — a strong, decisive no. “You will not have dominion over me (Romans 6:14)!” No to that thought, image, or memory. T: Turn your mind to another compelling reality. featured.title_zh: 教导子女了解那些被差遣的人
featured.content: It was a great honor to be able to partner with Missionary to create Goers , a series of illustrated biographies for children. Each biography introduces young readers and listeners to the stories of men and women who were sent by churches to spread the good news about Jesus Christ to the ends of the earth. Each is illustrated by the ultra-talented Rommel Ruiz. The books can be purchased as a set of three or as individual volumes. The Plowboy’s Bible: The Story of William Tyndale’s English Translation . Hunted by spies, William Tyndale fled across Europe with a bounty on his head, his Bible translation labeled as contraband. Young John, on the other hand, has a long day of farm work ahead of him. Although their lives seem worlds apart, John’s father knows a story that binds John and William together—their love for God’s word. The scripture John relies on for encouragement cost William everything, but they gave John’s family everything! Rescued from Darkness: Amy Carmichael and the Girls of Dohnavur . Kumari is scared, helpless, and alone in a dark temple until Amma, a mysterious woman from a faraway land, carries her away to a beautiful garden. This is not a fairy tale. It’s the true story of missionary Amy Carmichael and the children she rescued and raised at Dohnavur Fellowship in India. Into the Unknown: David Livingstone’s Heart for Africa . Before David Livingstone was the most famous man in the world, he was a boy who dreamed of being free to explore God’s creation. But when David reached the mission field, he found that freedom taken from the people he tried to teach about the Creator. This is the story of a goer’s dangerous journey to the ends of the earth, of his courageous stand for justice, and of his patient endurance for the sake of Christ. featured.title_zh: 我们的刑事司法制度在哪些方面存在缺陷（与Matt Martens合著）
featured.content: When you really want to dive into the details of big questions about public policy—how we can live better together—you run into two problems: The experts and other stakeholders don’t want to consider Christian arguments, and Christians don’t want to engage in the details. That combination of a Christian argument from a legal expert was rare when Matt Martens’s book Reforming Criminal Justice: A Christian Proposal came out in 2023 from Crossway. And it’s still rare today. Matt is a trial lawyer and partner at an international law firm in Washington, DC. He and his wife are members at Capitol Hill Baptist Church, and they have two sons and a daughter. I read this book when it came out, and it’s stuck with me. Just the other day, I was thinking about the book when talking to one of my pastors, who was preparing to preach from 1 Peter on justice and obeying authorities. I thought about how I’d want to see the criminal justice system reformed if there were a good shot I’d be either a victim or criminal defendant. Isn’t that the law summed up in loving our neighbors as ourselves? From the death penalty to AI to the decline of violent crime—Matt and I covered a great deal. featured.title: Small-Church Elders, Here’s How to Give Your Pastor a Sabbatical
featured.summary: Our church has 74 members and two lay elders. Here’s how we raised up five men to preach seven expository sermons and give our pastor a summer sabbatical.
featured.summary_zh: 我们的教会共有74名会友和两名平信徒长老。以下是我们如何培养五位弟兄来宣讲七篇解经性讲道，并让我们的牧师度过一个夏季安息假。
featured.title_zh: 小型教会的长老们，以下是为你们的牧师安排安息假的方式
featured.content: “He should have had a sabbatical six years ago,” my fellow elder said. “I know,” I said. “We know he needs it, but how are we going to do this? We have full-time jobs and young families.” “Well, the cattle on thousand hills are the Lord’s. Let’s ask him to provide it.” I nodded in agreement, but honestly, cattle felt like less of an ask for our church. Our church consists of 74 members. We have one full-time pastor and two lay elders. And yet, exactly two years after that initial elders’ meeting, we managed to give our pastor a much-needed, six-week summer sabbatical. Five male members of our church delivered seven expository and Christ-exalting sermons. God was glorified, our pastor rested, and our church loved it. We preached through an entire book of the Bible (Habakkuk). We preached a doctrinal sermon from our confession of faith (on baptism and Communion). Two men preached for the first time. The men ranged from age 20 to 46, and I was the seasoned preacher with 25 sermons under my belt. So how did we pull this off? 1. We prayed. We knew we couldn’t do this. Only God could. This reality framed our prayers over the next two years. God was glorified, our pastor rested, and our church loved it. We came to realize that just as the Sabbath was a gift from God to man (Mark 2:27), so a sabbatical is a gift from God to a pastor. As lay elders, we were called to take steps of faith to this end while relying on the Holy Spirit’s leading and enablement. Just as Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath (Matt. 12:8), so too is he Lord of a sabbatical. As we began to make plans, we prayed that we’d hold them with an open hand and continually lay them at the feet of Jesus. We borrowed words from Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 20:12) for our prayer in this season: “Lord, we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” 2. We planned backward. We began by identifying the ideal time of year for the sabbatical. We landed on July and August, since that’s when church programming is minimal and vacations are in vogue among our congregation. This decision indirectly led us to the length of sabbatical we felt could responsibly plan for: six weeks. From there, we planned backward. The first Sunday we discussed was the Sunday our pastor would return. How did we want our brother and his wife to reintegrate into the church? We decided we wanted him to feel the warmth of our church’s love in his homecoming without being distracted by sermon preparation. So we chose to begin and end his sabbatical on Fridays. This meant our pastor had a workweek before leaving, so he could help with administrative functions. And by returning from the sabbatical on a Friday, he’d be able to join us for an elder meeting to get updates on members prior to attending church two days later. Preaching could wait another week. We created a two-year timeline that included all of the specific events and developments we thought could be feasible with the Lord’s help. This timeline helped us to answer several looming questions: Should we start the sabbatical by sending our pastor somewhere to create physical and emotional separation between him and our congregation? We agreed we should. We also felt this was an opportunity to invite our church to be generous and to tangibly show their love to our pastor of 12 years and his wife by paying for this trip. How many of our male members would be willing to assist with the preaching? We estimated three to four. How and when would we get them trained? This was the hardest question to answer but also the most rewarding part of this process. 3. We created a brotherhood. We realized our biggest hurdle would be recruiting and training men to aid in the preaching. To address the issue, we settled on offering a six-week preaching cohort during the summer prior to the sabbatical. To identify potential men for the cohort, we asked, “Which men currently do Scripture readings and prayers exceptionally well in our worship services?” Then we talked to each man indiv
featured.content_zh:

12: 8),他也是安息日的主. 当我们开始计划时, 我们祈祷我们用开阔的手抓住他们, 我们在本季的祈祷中借用了Jehoshaphat(2 Chron. 20:12)的话,他说:我们的主啊!我们不知道该怎么办,但我们的眼睛在注视着你。 2. 我们计划落后。 我们首先确定了每年安息日的理想时间。

我们于7月和8月登陆, 这一决定间接导致了我们感到可以负责任地规划六个星期的休假时间。 从那里,我们计划向后。 我们讨论的第一个星期日 是牧师回来的星期日

这个时间表帮助我们回答了几个迫在眉睫的问题: 我们是否应该开始安息日,派牧师去某地,在肉体和情感上建立他和我们的会众之间的分离? 我们说好的 我们还觉得这是一个机会,邀请我们的教会慷慨解囊,并通过支付这次旅行的费用,向我们12年的牧师和他的妻子实际展示他们的爱意。

我们有多少男性成员愿意协助传道? 我们估计3到4个 我们如何和何时培训他们? 这是最难回答的问题,也是这一进程中最有价值的部分。 3. 我们建立了兄弟关系。 我们意识到我们的最大障碍是招募和训练人员来协助传道。

为了解决这一问题,我们决定在安息日之前的夏天提供六周的传教班。 我们问道,为了确定这群人中的潜在男子,“现在哪些人在我们的礼拜仪式中特别善于阅读和祈祷?” 然后我们和每个人交谈

featured.title_zh: 我们对耶稣的眼泪有什么误解
featured.content: Audio Transcript “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). It’s the shortest verse in the Bible. We read it together in the Navigators Bible Reading Plan yesterday. But it’s so brief we can pass it too quickly. Maybe we pass over it because we think we know what it means. Jesus’s friend Lazarus died. Jesus wept because his friend was gone. But what if we got that wrong? Or, what if we mistakenly thought his emotions were simple when they were complex? What if Jesus wept not simply in the loss of death but from a frustration with the living? Today on Ask Pastor John: what we get wrong about the tears of Jesus. Henry, a listener, writes in with a timely question on John 11:35. “Pastor John, thank you for taking my question today. I’d like to ask you about John 11:35. Why do you think Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus? One way to read this account is that he’s simply sharing in Mary and Martha’s sorrows over his death. But I wonder if something deeper is going on here. Jesus already planned to raise Lazarus, and he even told his disciples he was going to do it in John 11:11–15. “So, my questions are these two: First, why does Jesus ask, ‘Where have you laid him?’ Was he simply asking to be taken to the tomb? When they answer, ‘Lord, come and see,’ it’s almost like they still don’t appreciate who he is as the Messiah. And that is my second question: This whole event leaves me wondering if this weeping is more like Jesus’s weeping over Jerusalem in Luke 19:41 — weeping because he is heartbroken over the city’s unbelief. Is it a stretch to connect these two moments? Is Jesus grieving the dead Lazarus? Or is he grieving the unbelief of the living?” Jesus’s Mingled Emotions I doubt that any of Jesus’s emotions were simple. I think they were always complex. We finite creatures have emotions that respond to one or two, maybe three, happy or painful aspects of a situation. So, we may feel sorrow and joy mingled because, say, a very old saint has just gone to be with the Lord, and we will miss him, and yet we’re so happy for him. But Jesus could see every angle, every imaginable aspect of a situation, some of which called for very different emotions. So, I doubt that he ever had a simple emotion. For example, in Mark 3:1–5, there’s this man with a withered hand in the synagogue, and the people are watching to see if Jesus would heal him so that they could accuse Jesus. Can you imagine? They don’t give a hoot about this man’s pain. All they want is to accuse Jesus if he heals him. And in verse 5, it says, “He looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart.” And that’s what I mean by complex emotions: anger and grief perfectly mingled in the sinless heart of Jesus. Another example would be that he looked on unbelieving Jerusalem and wept: “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes” (Luke 19:42). But in Luke 10:21, it says Jesus “rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.’” He could weep and rejoice over the wise and bitter providence of God. So, we come to John 11 and the death of Lazarus. And I think Henry, who’s sending us this question, is right when he says Jesus’s tears in John 11 aren’t just about sharing our human grief — that maybe he is genuinely mourning their spiritual blindness. Yes, and I’m going to say not just mourning — he’s indignant. Divine Love and Wisdom The story begins in John 11:1–6 with Mary and Martha sending words to Jesus that their brother Lazarus is very sick. Jesus waits two more days before going and intentionally lets Lazarus die. " 耶稣哭泣 " (John 11:35)。 这是圣经中最短的一首诗。 我们昨天一起在《航海家圣经阅读计划》上读到的。 但时间太短了, 也许我们通过它,因为我们认为 我们知道它意味着什么。 耶稣的朋友拉扎鲁斯去世. 耶稣因为朋友不在而哭泣. 但如果我们搞错了呢?

或者,如果我们错误地认为 他的情绪是简单的 当它们是复杂的? 如果耶稣不仅在死亡中哭泣,而且在对活人的挫折中哭泣呢? 今天在"问约翰牧师"(Pastor John):我们对于耶稣的眼泪有什么错误. 亨利是一位听众,他及时写下约翰11:35的问题. “约翰神父,谢谢你今天接受我的问题。

featured.title: ‘I Was a Child of War’: How to Help Abuse Survivors Understand the Past
featured.summary: Yes, we were weak, but we were warriors, not victims.
featured.summary_zh: 是的，我们很弱小，但我们是战士，不是受害者。
featured.title_zh: “我曾是战争的孩子”：如何帮助虐待幸存者理解过去
featured.content: I grew up in a violent home, and it took me decades to find terms and categories that finally let me understand that aspect of my childhood. My first conversation partners and readings said I was a victim of abuse, but that framing was too passive to resonate with me. I believe the passive voice is valid, even essential. But when I discovered another framework, the child of war, I finally began to understand my past. Personal History That Led to Thoughts of War My father was a gifted professional, a compelling speaker who also possessed a shrewd wisdom. My mother seemed like a match—gifted, educated, and kind. But he was violent, even though for 16 years he was a pastor, and my mother couldn’t contain him. His behavior was our family secret, and if I hoped to understand it, I was on my own. Eventually, I read stories about one-dimensional moral monsters called “abusers”; their children were “victims.” But my parents seemed too admirable to be monsters, and the idea that I was a passive victim didn’t label my experience. I left home at 16 and essentially forgot the past until the month my father died. At that point, my readings on war let me see that my childhood had much in common with people who tried to resist and endure the aggression of a superior power. Terms like “resistance,” “war,” and “agency” fit better. They fostered understanding and healing. My first sharp memory is as ragged as a torn fingernail. Four years old, I’m hiding in my mother’s closet, behind dresses that smell of dust and skin cream. My skin stings and a deep ache runs beneath the surface. I’ve been spanked enough to know how it feels, but this is different. I think, I did something wrong, but what? I must deserve this, but why did he hit me so hard? Why does it hurt . . . so . . . much? I’m baffled by what we call mistreatment and betrayal. Fifty years later, I realized that 4-year-olds shouldn’t have the ability or experience to reflect critically on their beatings. And yet, because I could judge his actions, I could separate myself from him—he was “the” father rather than “my” father—and that gave me agency. When I turned 7, my favorite birthday gift was a miniature cowboy wagon. It was cheap, and the father quickly detected a flaw in the plastic. “This will snap,” he declared. He tugged and pulled at it until it broke, then he handed me the pieces and said, “See, I told you that would happen.” The playground had taught me that this was cruelty, so I decided to feel nothing , to sever his capacity to wound me. It was a foolish vow, one no child can fully keep, but it gave me a sense of agency or control. Two years later, it paid off. The chief gift for my 9th birthday was a basketball. When he decided I liked it too much, he stabbed it with a long knife. But by then, I’d hardened myself enough (agency again) to feel no grief, no surprise. It registered as a problem: Where would I get the money to buy another ball? How would I keep it safe? Because I could judge my father’s actions, I could separate myself from him, and that gave me agency. As time passed, my older brother and I began to resist him. We wore thick jeans when it seemed a belt might begin to fly. If a blow landed? Physical pain usually doesn’t last long. Social pains were tougher. The family moved often, because the father could always get a job but was too erratic to keep one. I attended five schools in seven years, chiefly in insular towns. I discovered that my athletic skills let me make friends through one team or another. Yet it was wise to mask my academic abilities-—unless the boys needed a math champion to wipe the smirks off the smart girls’ faces. I was making a way, until the dynamics at home shifted. Perhaps it was the alcohol. Perhaps it was the professional failure. The father was now reduced to the oversight of a tiny country church, two part-time jobs, and summer work for the Red Cross. Whatever the reasons, his behavior became ominous. He cursed and raged day after day,

我在一个暴力的家庭里长大,我花了几十年的时间才找到最终让我理解我童年的这一方面的术语和类别. 我的第一个谈话伙伴和读者说,我是虐待的受害者,但这种陷害太被动,无法与我产生共鸣。 我认为被动的声音是有效的,甚至是必不可少的。

但当我发现另一个框架,战争的孩子, 我终于开始理解我的过去。 个人历史 我父亲是一位有天赋的专业人士,一位很有说服力的演讲者,他拥有精明的智慧。 我妈妈看起来是一对配对, 虽然他16年来都是牧师,

他的行为是我们家族的秘密, 如果我希望理解它,我独自一人。 最终,我读到了关于一维道德怪物的故事,称为“滥用者 ” ; 他们的孩子是“受害者 ” 。 但我的父母似乎太令人钦佩了,

我16岁离开家 基本上忘记了过去 直到我父亲去世的那个月 那时,我对战争的解读让我看到,我的童年与那些试图抵抗和忍受一个超级大国的侵略的人们有许多共同点。 " 抵抗 " 、 " 战争 " 和 " 机构 " 等用语比较合适。 它们促进了理解和愈合。 我的第一个尖锐的记忆就像一个撕裂的手指甲一样

我躲在母亲的衣柜里, 我的皮肤刺痛 和深深的痛 运行在地表之下。 但情况不同。 我想,我做错了什么? 我必须得这样 但他为什么打我这么重? 为什么这么痛?

我对所谓的虐待和背叛感到困惑。 50年后,我意识到4岁的孩子不应该有批判性地反思殴打他们的能力或经验。 然而,因为我可以判断他的行为,我可以把自己与他分开——他是“父亲”而不是“我的父亲”,这给了我代理权。

当我七岁的时候 我最喜欢的生日礼物是一辆小型牛仔车 它很便宜,父亲很快发现了塑料的缺陷. 他宣称,“这将崩溃”。

他拉着它,拉着它,直到它破碎,然后他把碎片递给我,他说:你看,我告诉你了。 游乐场告诉我,这是残酷的, 所以我决定没有任何感觉, 切断他伤害我的能力。 这是一个愚蠢的誓言,一个没有孩子能完全保持的,但它给了我一种代理感或控制感. 两年之后,它得到了回报。

我九岁生日的主要礼物是篮球 当他决定我太喜欢它时 他用长刀刺它 但到那时,我已使自己变得足够坚固(又是一个机构),不感到悲伤,也不感到惊讶。 它是一个问题: 我哪来的钱买另一球? 我怎么保证它的安全?

因为我可以判断我父亲的行为, 随着时间流逝,我和哥哥开始反抗他. 我们穿着厚厚的牛仔裤 当它看起来可能开始飞翔。 如果一击落地? 身体疼痛通常不会持续很长时间。 社会痛苦更严重。

家里人经常搬家,因为父亲总是可以找到工作,但是过于不稳定,无法保留工作。 我在七年中就读了五所学校,主要在岛屿城镇。 我发现我的运动能力 让我通过一个或另一个团队交朋友。 除非男生需要数学冠军来抹去聪明女孩脸上的笑容,

我在想办法 直到家里的动态变化 也许是因为酒 也许是职业上的失败 父亲现在被降格为一个小乡村教会的监督,两个兼职工作,以及红十字会的暑期工作. 不管是什么原因 他的行为变得不祥 他日复一日的诅咒和愤怒,

featured.title: How to Preach to Workers
featured.summary: The New Testament offers two paradigms for how preachers can consider workers in their teaching.
featured.summary_zh: 新约提供了两种范式，说明传道人如何在教导中考虑到工人。
featured.title_zh: 如何向工人传福音
featured.content: I still remember the first time I heard a sermon on God’s design for work. Pastor Colin Smith was in a series working through the Ten Commandments, and he’d come to the fourth command about the Sabbath. I was expecting to hear challenging words about rest. So I was surprised when he spent the first half of his sermon talking about work. Because he’s a good exegetical preacher, Smith reminded us to pay attention to the part of the passage we might overlook: “Six days you shall labor, and do all your work . . .” (Ex. 20:9). For 16 minutes, Smith preached about God’s design for work. He explained how God modeled work in creation, crafting and making our world like a builder, engineer, and artist. And since humans were created in the likeness of this God, our labors are a significant part of what it means to represent him in the world. Then he started naming regular kinds of work—such as the school crossing guard who creates a zone of safety and protection for children. He shared example after example, even naming those who are were unemployed and looking for work as engaging in a form of dignified labor. They can please God as they trust him to provide and remain diligent to seek out what’s next. At the time, I was working a summer landscaping job between semesters at seminary. I took the job because it was necessary, not because I found it personally fulfilling or spiritually significant. I’d been subconsciously wanting to be done with mowing lawns and picking weeds so I could get back to the important work of studying Scripture. But God used Smith’s sermon to reorient my ordinary labor. Preaching with workers in mind is vital to shepherding a congregation. It reminds church members that work is a primary context for discipleship and helps them work out the implications of God’s Word where they spend a large portion of their time. The New Testament gives two paradigms for how preachers can consider workers in their teaching. Work as an Illustration of the Kingdom As the eternal, perfect Son of God, Jesus isn’t only Savior and Lord but also the most brilliant teacher the world has ever heard. Therefore, as preachers, we take his pedagogy seriously even as we learn his precepts and mimic his practices. Jesus often proclaims the good news by igniting people’s imaginations and explaining eternal truths in concrete realities, including the body (Matt. 6:22; 7:3–5; 24:7–8), nature (Matt. 6:28–29; Mark 11:23; Luke 17:6), and food (Matt. 13:33; John 6:35, 53–56). But Jesus’s most consistent metaphor for the truths of the kingdom is work and workers. Klaus Issler’s survey reveals that of the 37 parables in the Synoptic Gospels, 32 reference work or workers, representing 22 different work roles. In 25 of the parables, work is a main part of the storyline. Here are examples: The farmer sows the seed (Matt. 13). The faithful manager gives the servants of the household food at the proper time (Luke 12:42). Even an unjust judge will give a persistent widow justice (18:1–8). The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). A king going into battle should take counsel to see if he’s strong enough before he a ttacks (Luke 14:31). When Jesus describes what it meant to follow him and live in his kingdom, why does he use the ordinary language of work and workers? First, God’s self-disclosure is often wrapped in the language of work. For instance, he’s portrayed as a composer and performer (Deut. 31:19), a tentmaker (Job 9:8), a garment maker and dresser (29:14), a shepherd (Ps. 23:1–4), a builder (Prov. 8:27–31), a metalworker (Isa. 1:24–26), a potter (31:9), and a farmer (Hos. 10:11). 我还记得我第一次听到关于上帝设计工作的布道。 科林·史密斯牧师在"十诫"系列中工作, 我希望听到关于休息的富有挑战性的话。 他上半场讲道工作时 我感到惊讶

由于他是一个优秀的传教士,史密斯提醒我们注意我们可能忽略的那段话:"六天你必须努力,并做你所有的工作."(前20:9). 16分钟,史密斯宣扬上帝的工作设计. 他解释了上帝如何塑造我们的世界 像一个建筑师、工程师和艺术家

由于人类是在这个上帝的相似之处创造的, 我们的劳动是世界中代表他的意义的重要部分. 然后,他开始点名从事常规工作,例如学校越野警卫,为儿童创造一个安全和保护的地区。

他举了个例子,甚至将那些失业和寻找工作的人命名为从事一种有尊严的劳动。 他们可以取悦上帝, 因为他们相信上帝提供, 当时我在神学院的暑期园林设计工作

我接受这份工作是因为有必要,而不是因为我发现这份工作是个人的满足或精神意义。 我潜意识地想要完成割草和摘草, 但上帝用史密斯的布道来调整我的普通劳动。 向工人宣讲对牧羊人至关重要。

它提醒教会成员,工作是门徒活动的主要背景,帮助他们解决神话的影响,在那里他们花费了大量的时间. "新约"为传教士如何在教学中考虑工人给出了两种范式.

发挥王国的作用 耶稣不仅是救世主, 因此,作为传教士,我们在学习他的戒律和模仿他的做法时,也认真对待他的教学方法.

耶稣经常通过点燃人们的想象力和在具体现实中解释永恒的真理来宣告好消息,包括身体(Matt 6:22;7:3–5;24:7–8),自然(Matt 6:28–29;Mark 11:23;Luke 17:6)和食物(Matt 13:33;John 6:35,53–56). 但耶稣对王国真理最一致的比喻是工作和工人.

Klaus Issler的调查表明,在Synoptic福音书中的37个比喻中,有32个参考工作或工人,代表着22个不同的工作角色. 在25个比喻中,作品是故事情节的主要部分. 以下是例子:农民播种(Matt.13). 忠诚的经理在适当的时候给家庭食物的仆人(公爵12:42).

即使是不公正的法官也会给守寡者一个持久的公正(18:1-8)。 善牧者为羊舍命(约翰10:11). 一个参战的国王应该接受建议, 当耶稣描述追随他并生活在他的王国的意义时,他为什么使用普通的劳动和工人语言?

首先,上帝的自我披露常常用工作语言包扎。 例如,他被描绘成作曲家和表演者(德国31:19)、帐篷匠(约旦9:8)、制衣和梳妆师(29:14)、牧羊人(Ps.23:1-4)、建筑师(Prov.8:27-31)、金属工人(Isa:1:24-26)、锅工(31:9)和农民(Hos:10:11)。

featured.title_zh: 女性可以成为执事吗？
featured.content: ABSTRACT: Whether or not women can serve as deacons is a live question for many Christians, especially with more churches shifting from a deacon-led to an elder-led polity. The nature of the role, the example of Phoebe, and the qualifications for deacons in 1 Timothy 3 may allow room for deaconesses, but each of these arguments faces compelling counterarguments. In the absence of clear biblical evidence for women holding this formal office, wisdom leads Christians to approach the question with both conviction and charity. For our ongoing series of feature articles for pastors and Christian leaders, we asked Benjamin Merkle (PhD, The Southern Baptist Theological Seminary), Research Professor of New Testament and Greek at Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary, to examine the biblical evidence for women serving as deacons. By asking the question “Can women serve as deacons?” we are not simply asking whether women can serve the church. Scripture obviously permits and commends women serving the church. The question is whether the New Testament permits women to hold the formal office of deacon. Many churches are asking this question, for at least two reasons. First, women should not be restricted from serving in places where the Bible does not restrict them. If the Bible permits women to be deacons, then a church’s tradition does not offer sufficient grounds to prohibit them from holding the office. Women are essential to the health and vitality of the church, and we certainly don’t want to limit the church’s effectiveness over an unbiblical practice. Second, many churches either have moved or are moving to a plural-eldership model of church leadership. Historically, many Baptist, baptistic, or nondenominational churches were governed by a board of deacons. These deacons held leadership authority in a way that many believe is inappropriate for the office of deacon. For complementarians, it would not be wise for women to be deacons in such a context since it would violate 1 Timothy 2:12 (“I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man”). Under complementarianism, the relevant question is not whether an office possesses any authority whatsoever, but whether an office’s authority constitutes the kind of teaching or governing authority restricted to men. If a deacon holds elder-like authority, then, regardless of the title used, it would be wrong for a woman to hold the position because she would have authority over a man. If, however, a church has male elders who have authority to lead the church, then some are asking if it would be permissible to allow women to be deacons since a deacon is a position with little to no authority. With hundreds of churches shifting from a deacon-led to an elder-led polity, the question of whether women can be deacons becomes relevant. This essay unfolds as follows. I present the three best views for allowing women to be deacons. 1 (I assume a complementarian framework. The egalitarian-versus-complementarian debate is important, but I will not address it here.) After presenting each argument in favor of women deacons, I provide counterarguments. Although there are reasonable arguments for allowing women to serve as deacons, this essay argues that the New Testament provides no clear text that permits women to hold the office of deacon. I conclude the essay with three principles to keep in mind when dealing with this issue in the local church. Argument 1: The Nature of the Office The first argument for allowing women to hold the office of deacon concerns the nature of the office itself: Deacons are servants and not leaders. 2 As servants, deacons do not possess authority but serve the church in low-key (though important) ways. Consequently, nothing in Scripture would prohibit women from holding this office. The elders (also called “overseers” or “pastors”) are given the task of teaching and leading the church. ABSTRACT:妇女是否可以担任执事是许多基督徒的活生生的问题,特别是更多的教会从执事转向长者领导的政体。 角色的性质,菲比的例子,以及1 Timothy 3中的执事资格,可能为执事留有余地,但这些论点都面临着令人信服的反驳.

在没有明确的圣经证据证明妇女担任这一正式职务的情况下,智慧促使基督教徒以信念和慈善的态度对待这个问题。

对于我们目前为牧师和基督教领袖发表的一系列专题文章,我们请本杰明·梅尔克勒(PhD, The Southern Baptist Theocational Seminary),新约研究教授和东南浸信会神学院的希腊人,为担任执事的妇女审查圣经证据.

通过问“妇女能否担任执事?” 我们不仅仅是问妇女是否能够为教会服务。 圣经显然允许和赞扬为教会服务的妇女。 问题是新约是否允许妇女担任正式执事职务. 许多教会提出这个问题,至少有两个原因。

第一,不应限制妇女在圣经没有限制的地方服务。 如果《圣经》允许妇女担任执事,那么教会的传统就不足以禁止她们担任公职。 女性对教会的健康与活力至关重要,

第二,许多教堂要么已经搬迁,要么正在转向教会领导的多元-老年模式。 历史上,许多浸信会,洗礼会,或非宗派教会都由执事委员会管理. 这些执事以许多人认为不适合执事办公室的方式掌握领导权.

对于辅助者来说,在这样的背景下由妇女担任执事是不明智的,因为这将违反1 Timothy 2:12(“我不允许妇女教授或对男子行使权力”)。

在补充主义下,相关问题不是办公室是否拥有任何权威,而是办公室的权威是否构成仅限于男性的教学或管理权威。 如果执事拥有长者般的权威,那么,不管使用的头衔如何,女性担任这一职务是错误的,因为她将对男性拥有权威.

但是,如果一个教会有男性长者有权领导教会,那么有些人会问是否允许妇女担任执事,因为执事是一个几乎没有权力或没有权力的职位。 随着数百个教堂从执事转向长者领导的政体,妇女是否可以担任执事的问题变得重要. 这篇散文展开如下.

我提出三种最佳观点,允许妇女担任执事。 1(我假设是一个补充框架。) 平等与互补的辩论很重要,但我不想在这里谈论。 ) 在提出每一个有利于女性执事的论据后,我提出反驳.

虽然有合理的理由允许女性担任执事,但是这篇文章认为,新约没有给出允许女性担任执事的明确文本. 最后,我提出三项原则,以便在当地教会处理这一问题时铭记这些原则。

论点1:办公室的性质 允许妇女担任执事职位的第一个论点涉及办公室本身的性质:执事是仆人而不是领导者。 2个 作为仆人,执事并不拥有权威,而是以低调(虽然重要)的方式为教会服务. 因此,《圣经》中没有任何内容禁止妇女担任这一职务。

featured.content: I have been blogging at Challies.com on a daily basis for over 23 years now. That long commitment has allowed me to write thousands of articles and hundreds of book reviews while also sending millions of visitors to other sites through the daily A La Carte feature. Though I’ve also written a number of books, the blog has always remained the “main thing.” Much of the blog’s content is now also translated into Spanish , French , and a number of other languages. One of my great desires has always been to freely give away as much as possible. I intend for it to always remain entirely free for all who visit . While, for obvious reasons, this can’t happen when it comes to books, I’ve made it my goal to ensure that everything else has been freely and widely distributed. While this has been possible largely because of advertisers, there is also a key role for the generosity of individuals. This is where patrons come in—patrons like you. There are a couple of different options for you to consider. The first is recurring monthly gifts. A service called Patreon provides a convenient means of linking content producers (like me) with ongoing supporters (like you). You can learn more and sign up at Patreon.com/challies . I also share monthly ministry and family updates there. The second is one-time gifts. If that is of interest to you, they can be made electronically via PayPal . If you prefer to send a one-time gift via check, you can simply mail a check (drawn on a US or Canadian bank) to this address: Tim Challies 1011 Upper Middle Road East, Box #1214 Oakville, Ontario L6H 5Z9 Canada Funds donated will be used to support my family and to help create great content or to otherwise improve, support, and enhance Challies.com. In one way or another, they will all be used to allow me to continue to do what I have been doing for these past 23+ years. Please understand that I intend for Challies.com to always remain entirely free. In fact, patrons help ensure that it always remains that way. Thank you for considering becoming a patron of Challies.com. Your support means so much to me. And this is the end of my once-yearly mention of this subject! featured.title_zh: 你不能就说耶稣爱我吗？
featured.content: “Hold the lettuce.” The simple sentence, perhaps stated more frequently than we might hope, captures a crucial hallmark that predominates in the thinking of many. At a recent lunch with a friend, I saw this firsthand. For my friend, it wasn’t just the lettuce. The instructions he gave restrained the cook from adding anything remotely vegetable-like to the hamburger. Notwithstanding my jibe, my friend held fast to his decision. He was the one ordering. And he expected (rightly so!) to be served what he desired. After all, the customer is king. This cluster of expectations animates the modern marketplace. We want products tailored to our specific needs. We seek out services that let us pay only for what we want. We get frustrated when we take the car to a mechanic who not only fixes the problem we knew about but also takes the liberty of repairing other problems (and charging liberally for them). In short, we want (and expect) to be served according to our preferences and felt needs. Innocuous enough when it comes to the morsels on our plates, the reign of personal preferences involves more serious implications when it extends over the rest of life. And in the life of faith, the consequences are serious indeed. For preference-driven faith will, in the end, produce a Christless Christianity. Have It Your Way What do we hope for when we join the church for worship? Parsing motives presents no easy project, especially if there are children in tow or responsibilities for some aspect of the service or fellowship. Few of us have the personal or cognitive space to search out the depths of our hearts en route to the Sunday morning service. But the way home often presents opportunities to interrogate those hidden recesses. The questions we pose shed light on what is in our hearts: “How did you like the sermon this morning?” “Didn’t the worship team nail it today?” We tend to ask not about a confrontation with gospel truth but about measures of personal satisfaction. If our questions begin illuminating this tendency, the answers we give put our motives on clear display: “I thought the pastor did a great job! I really liked . . .” or “Ya know, I just wasn’t feeling it this morning; the sermon didn’t really speak to me.” “Yes, the worship was great!” or “I thought the team was a bit off. Did you hear them mess up on that one song?” So often, whether at the sandwich shop or on the way home from church, preference-driven language bubbles out of our mouths like boiling water from an unwatched pot. For many, our post-service concerns center far too frequently on how well certain aspects of the service met our felt needs. What did I gain from the sermon? Did I enjoy the music? Service to the ascendant self predominates. We reflect on the worship gathering in a manner unsettlingly similar to how we might reflect on a hamburger: It was decent, but I’ve had better elsewhere. I think they overdid the mayonnaise, and I would have preferred sesame rather than a brioche bun. Whether we want to admit it or not, our expectations of being served as we please spill into our perceived relationship to the church’s gathered worship. Those same expectations shape how we approach our Lord. We tend naturally, in our sin, to want merely an affirming savior. We like to hear that Jesus loves sinners so much that he died to win them, for hearing this affirms that our need for forgiveness has been met. We like to hear that his love for his sheep never falters, for hearing this quells the fear that perhaps our snide words or dubious choices or the train wreck of our inner thoughts might put our hope in jeopardy. We like to hear how our Lord railed against the hypocrisy and legalism of the Pharisees, for hearing this makes us smile inwardly, pleased that we are not so pretentious and uptight. Messages such as these leave us content, unruffled, ready to carry on with life as normal, affirmed in our preferred way of life by a (truncated) gospel that accomplishes little b
featured.content_zh:
“抓住生菜。” 这个简单的句子,也许比我们所希望的更频繁地说,抓住了在许多人的思想中占主导地位的关键标志。 最近和一个朋友共进午餐时 我亲眼看到的 对我的朋友来说, 他给厨师的指示 禁止在汉堡里添加任何类似蔬菜的东西

我的朋友坚持他的决定 是他订的 他希望自己所欲达到的, 毕竟客为王. 这一组期望激发出现代市场。 我们需要适合我们具体需要的产品。 我们寻求服务,让我们只为所欲为。

我们感到沮丧的是,我们把车送到一个技工那里,他不仅解决了我们所知道的问题,而且还自由地修复了其他问题(并且对这些问题收取宽松的费用)。 简言之,我们希望(并期望)根据我们的喜好和感受到的需要得到服务。

谈到我们盘子里的泥潭时,个人偏好的统治,如果延续到余生,就会产生更严重的影响。 在信仰的生活中,后果确实很严重。 因为受偏好驱使的信仰,最终会产生出一种没有基督的基督教. 我们加入教堂做礼拜时希望什么?

分析动机并非易事,特别是如果有儿童被拖走或承担某些方面的服务或研究金责任。 我们当中很少有人拥有个人或认知空间,在前往周日早间礼拜的路上去探寻内心深处. 但回家的方式往往为审讯那些隐蔽的休庭提供了机会。

我们提出的问题揭示了我们心中的心事,“你今天早上喜欢讲道吗?” 我们往往不问与福音真相的对抗,而是问个人满意的措施。 如果我们的问题开始说明这一趋势,我们给出的答案清楚地显示了我们的动机:“我认为牧师做了一件伟大的工作!

我真的很喜欢. . . . . . . . . “是的,崇拜是伟大的!”或“我认为队伍有点偏差。 你听到他们把那首歌弄乱了吗?” 所以,无论是在三明治店,还是在从教堂回家的路上,偏好驱动的语言泡从我们嘴里喷出,就像从一个无人观察的锅中取出沸水来.

对许多人来说,我们的服务后关切过于频繁地集中在服务的某些方面在多大程度上满足了我们的需要。 我从布道中得到什么? 我很喜欢音乐吗? 服务于上层的自我占主导地位。 我们以令人不安的方式思考礼拜聚会, 但我在别处生活得更好。

我觉得他们做了蛋黄酱, 我更喜欢芝麻,而不是布洛克包。 无论我们是否愿意承认这一点,我们期望得到服务,因为我们希望与教会所聚集的礼拜的感同身受。 同样的期望决定了我们如何接近我们的主。 我们的罪孽中,自然而然地只想要一个坚定的救世主。

我们喜欢听到耶稣如此地爱罪人,以至于他为了赢得他们的胜利而去死,因为听到这个消息,肯定了我们对宽恕的需要已经得到满足了. 我们想听到,他对他的羊的爱从未动摇,因为听到这种平息的恐惧,也许我们的暗语或可疑的选择,或者我们内心思想的火车残骸会使我们的希望陷入危险.

我们想听听我们的主如何反对法利赛人的虚伪和法西斯主义,因为听到这使我们对内微笑,很高兴我们没有这么自大和紧张。 这样的讯息给我们留下了内容,没有磨损,准备继续正常生活,在我们所偏爱的生活方式中,用一个(经磨练的)福音来证实,这些福音成就不大。

featured.content: Thanks for reading A La Carte! I’ve got a good collection of articles, sales, deals, and other material for you this morning. I hope you enjoy it! Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a new edition of John Piper’s Desiring God , two reader-friendly studies in Romans from Tim Keller, The Gospel After Christendom , and my own From the Rising of the Sun (which, to remind you, includes the full documentary for free). Westminster Books is featuring my three Goers books for kids, each of which features a well-known Christian figure. They are nicely discounted. Logos users will want to check out Bible Study Week where you’ll find lots of deals, highlighted by the Tyndale OT & NT Commentaries at $4.99 each. Recommended Reading The Hardest Day You May Ever Face. This is a beautifully tragic piece of writing from Kimberly Wagner as she recounts an extremely hard day. “Daylight was just breaking over the ridge beyond the hills when I slipped into Mom’s bedroom and climbed into the bed beside her, the same bed that as a child I’d run to in the middle of the night to find safety and comfort. On this date, many years ago, we laid my dad’s body in the grave. But, Momma no longer remembers dates, or only guesses to know what season of the year we’re in. She won’t know the significance of today’s date, but she does have a foggy awareness that, to her today represents something terrible on her horizon.” For the Ones Like Me. Zachary Conover writes for those who are like him in that they were raised as good church kids. “What does it mean that we were dead in our trespasses and sins? How were we enemies of God? How were our hearts in rebellion against His Word? For students who have grown up attending church, reading the Bible, and learning about Jesus, these descriptions can be difficult to reconcile with their own experience. I understand that difficulty because I was one of those kids.” Praying to the God Who Rules History. Casey McCall reminds us that when we pray, we pray to the God who rules history. “If your doctrine of God leads you to pray less, you need to reevaluate your understanding of God. If your system of theology leads you to underemphasize the practical power of petitionary prayer in your life, you need to modify your system.” Dear Gen Alpha, Claude Wants to Turn You Into a Toad. Please, for the Love of All Things Human, Don’t Let It. Christina Bieber Lake warns members of Gen Alpha about what an all-out and unthoughtful commitment to Claude and other AI apps is likely to do to them. “In simple terms, we are moving from AI (Artificial Intelligence), which is about getting help processing information, to AGI (Artificial General Intelligence), which is about telling a machine what to do and letting it do it while you sit back and file your fingernails. Experts are saying that AGI will produce ten times the impact of the industrial revolution at ten times the speed.” Old Dogs and New Tricks. “I’m not opposed to the idea of people retiring after many decades of work. They have worked hard, so why not enjoy the fruit of their labor? But what I’ve found disquieting is the static nature that characterizes some retirements. I’ve seen some light, however, at the end of the tunnel and from where I stand, it doesn’t look like a train!” J.V. Fesko explains why he isn’t eager to retire, even if he does eventually withdraw from the front lines of work. Getting a Handle on Our Emotions. Writing for the Biblical Counseling Coalition, Esther St. John offers counsel on getting a handle on emotions, or, perhaps better said, stewarding them faithfully. A Great Error Respecting Duty I have often pointed out that Christians used to speak of duty far more often than we do today, since it was important to express and fulfill the duties God had given his people. You can read what William Plumer believed about duty in this brief quote from one of his works, A Word to the Weary . God’s people sometimes fall into a great error respecting their duty.

featured.title_zh: 数千次家庭查经的累积效应
featured.content: The alarm goes off, and another busy day begins. Getting kids up and ready for school, meal prep, work, after-school activities. Before you know it, the day is racing to its close. And you’re exhausted again. As Christian parents, we want our lives to count for Christ. We sincerely want our children to live their lives for Christ too. We want them to be changed by the same amazing grace that has transformed us. But how does this happen? How can we find the time and energy to effectively disciple our kids? Where will we find the creativity and passion to teach them what matters most? If you’re discouraged by your limited time and ability to shepherd your children, consider the cumulative effects of thousands of family Bible readings over the course of many years. Think Small What if a brief Bible reading today, a couple more later this week, and a few more next week eventually became a pattern, a deeply rooted habit for your family? Small investments of time and intentionality can make a big difference over a couple decades. Small investments of time and intentionality can make a big difference over the span of a couple decades. Years ago, Trevin Wax wrote an article titled “ 1000 Sermons Will Change Your Life .” What he says to pastors about preaching also applies to parents who lead their kids in family Bible reading: Pastors, don’t underestimate the cumulative effect of your preaching. You are not dumping information into brains. You are forming the habits of your people, teaching them how to read and understand and apply the Bible for themselves. Similarly in family life, our discipleship has cumulative effects that may not come to fruition for years. As parents, we’re in this for the long haul. If your children live in your home from birth to age 18, that’s 6,570 days. If you read the Bible together on average every third day, that’s 2,190 Bible readings over the course of your sons’ and daughters’ childhood and teenage years. Keep that big picture in mind when you feel defeated after a couple days on the go, when those family discipleship moments have eluded you. Think of Timothy, who was acquainted with the sacred writings from childhood because of his mother’s and grandmother’s faithful witness (2 Tim. 1:5; 3:14–15). May we be influential parents like them, who little by little and day by day pass on our life of faith to the next generation. Be Consistent, Establish a Habit With the long view in mind, think small in terms of your goals for this week, month, or year. Aim for consistency, for establishing a habit that you can pray will take root in your kids’ lives. Joe Carter recently shared the results of a sociological study of how faith moves across generations. He summarized the findings: The behaviors that most strongly predict lasting faith are active and verbal: praying together as a family, saying grace, embedding faith in the rhythm of the week rather than reserving it for Sunday, and, above all, talking about it. Children raised in homes where faith was discussed at least several times a week were more than twice as likely to attend church, pray daily, and rate religion as very important in young adulthood. The simplest way to put this truth into practice in your home is by creating a rhythm of opening the Bible regularly, reading some verses, and discussing them. You may never have a sense that one particular devotional was transformative. But keep at it. When your kids are inattentive or disruptive, don’t be overly discouraged. If the milk spills, if a fight erupts, all is not lost. Resist the temptation to quit. Come back to the reading the next day, or the day after that. Keep finding times to open the Bible with your family. Let the Word Do the Heavy Lifting Another deterrent that may get in the way of family discipleship is “the intimidation factor.” If you feel ill-equipped to teach the Bible to your kids, you may be inclined to leave that task to Sunday school teachers and youth pastors. featured.title: In the Darkness, Christmas Shines a Light
featured.summary: The general revelation of God’s created order—darkness and light, night and day—primes every created thing to know they need light, a salvation from outside themselves.
featured.summary_zh: 神所创造的秩序——黑暗与光明、黑夜与白昼——的普遍启示，使每一受造物都认识到自己需要光明，需要来自自身之外的拯救。
featured.title_zh: 在黑暗中，圣诞节照亮光明
featured.content: Read For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will be seen upon you. And nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising. (Isa. 60:2–3) Reflect There’s something about a sunrise. It wakes the world. Unlike the jarring blare of an alarm clock, a sunrise quietly whispers “Wake, O sleeper” with the graceful love of a parent rubbing a sleeping child’s back. When the sun rises, the slumbering stir to life. We’ve just spent seven or eight hours dead to the world. Then the sunrise triggers in us what looks like a resurrection. We rise. Certain flowers—daisies, poppies, and the aptly named morning glories—open their blossoms at the sun’s rising. Little by little, empty streets fill and quiet houses stir. Drawn to the warmth and energy of the just-unveiled sun, we transition from rest to work, stillness to activity. Drawn to the warmth and energy of the just-unveiled sun, we transition from rest to work, stillness to activity. It’s not surprising that the sun is an oft-used metaphor for God. For he, too, resurrects the dead. He, too, is the Giver of life and growth. He, too, draws all things to himself—such as the trees, which by nature grow upward, toward the sun, their branches like arms raised in perpetual worship. This is the created order. All things were made to be drawn to and sustained by the sun. We were made to be alive insofar as we live, grow, and flourish by solar energy. So too with God. We’re in darkness and death without him. As he bestows his grace on us, we rise to new life. We’re able to grow. Like the sunflower blossom, which turns to follow the sun wherever it’s positioned in the sky, we’re created to look to the Lord, who “will arise upon [us], and his glory will be seen upon [us]” (Isa. 60:2). In a world of darkness, we ache for the light. We wait for the sunrise. All nations, all kings, all people share this in common. The horizon each of us looks to—the nature of the “new day” we await—may be different: A new job. A remodeled home. A regime change. But only the sunrise of Christ will eternally satisfy. His is “the true light, which gives light to everyone” (John 1:9). Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled in him. Only the sunrise of Christ will eternally satisfy. The general revelation of God’s created order—darkness and light, night and day—primes every created thing to know they need light, a salvation from outside themselves. The special revelation of Christ reveals a truer light than even the sun: the light that is our eternal life, the light the darkness will never overcome (v. 5), the light that will one day end night as we know it (Rev. 22:5). Respond How is God’s glory seen in your life? How are you reflecting his beauty? In contrast to those who dwell in darkness, how does your life reflect 1 Thessalonians 5:5: “You are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness”?

featured.title_zh: 如果家庭游戏之夜能让您的孩子谈论圣经，会怎么样？
featured.content: This week, the blog is sponsored by Doxa Games . This post is written by Marco Bartholomae, founder of Doxa Games and creator of the Bible-based board and card games Trials & Triumphs , Bible Clash , and Hurry! Fleeing Disciples . A couple of years ago, I was playing cards with my kids when a question hit me. What would it take to make a Bible game they’d ask to play again? I grew up in Germany with four brothers. We played cards on long car rides and spent hours on our bedroom floor with a board game spread out between us. I still remember how easy it was to lose track of time when we played together. Now I live in California with my wife and our four children, and we still love a good game night. The screens go away, somebody wants a rematch, and we get to enjoy being together. That question from the card table stayed with me. I started imagining games that could give other families that same experience and get them talking about Scripture along the way, games a child could sit down to, learn the rules, and enjoy right away, even if they were new to the Bible. Then maybe a name on a card or something that happened on the board would make them curious enough to ask a question. That’s how Doxa Games started. The Conversations That Start Around the Table In Deuteronomy 6, God tells his people to speak about his commandments with their children as they go about ordinary life, including when they sit at home. A game night gives us another chance to do that. Our games don’t replace family devotions, but they do open conversations about God’s Word. Your child might pick up a card and ask who Thaddaeus was. A race to a house church might get them wondering why the early Christians gathered in homes. Those are questions you can follow right back to Scripture. That’s also why I chose the name Doxa . It’s the Greek word for glory . In 1 Corinthians 10:31, Paul reminds us to do everything to the glory of God, even in ordinary things like eating and drinking. That conviction shapes what we make and how we think about time around the table. Three Games to Play With Your Family Bible Clash: Gospels (ages 8+) is a fast-paced, head-to-head card game. Play characters from the four Gospels and try to outscore your opponent. Trials & Triumphs (ages 5+) sends players down a winding path where one turn can move you forward, and the next can set you back. It gives younger kids a way to talk about trusting Christ through trials. Hurry! Fleeing Disciples (ages 8+) takes you into the world of Acts. Choose your route, evade Roman guards, and race to reach a house church. From Our Family Table to the Mission Field As Doxa grows, we hope to translate these games and put them in the hands of missionaries, church planters, and ministry training centers in places like Colombia, the Philippines, and East Africa. I’d love for a family in Malawi to pull out one of these games, play it in their own language, and have the same kinds of conversations we have around our table. If your family is getting together this Christmas, pick a game, clear a spot at the table, and let the kids make the first move. See all three games at DoxaGames.com . featured.title_zh: 如何在基督教组织中解雇某人
featured.content: Over the course of my career, I’ve participated in more than 190 exits of employees, whether I was coaching a manager, planning upstream, sitting in on calls, or orchestrating layoffs. Each time was tough. Parting ways with an employee is one of the heaviest things a manager does. Doing it both clearly and kindly takes a lot of preparation and emotional regulation. In a faith-based workplace, these decisions can be even more surprising and hurtful, because managers try to spare the discomfort of a conversation about performance under any number of banners of being “kind.” How should we think about this as Christians who manage other Christians? Why Good Work Is Important A church’s mission is to spread the good news of Jesus, create ways for people to know him more deeply, and love our neighbors. A Christian nonprofit’s purpose is adjacent—to provide mercy, justice, evangelism, or discipleship while pointing people to Christ and their local church. This work happens through ministry and outreach staff, but also through effective operations. Doing this work takes all types of roles: pastors, administrators, and ministry coordinators; managers, accountants, and musicians; executive admins, facilities operators, and IT teams. Much of what it takes to run a church or Christian organization happens outside the hours of direct ministry. To do any of this well, churches and nonprofits must hire capable people who can effectively perform their duties and steward the mission. When managers in a secular workplace don’t hire wisely, I’ve seen the result in poor functional performance, departmental infighting, disengagement, acrimonious exits, and abuse of company resources. In a faith-based organization or church, you may get a mix of this and something worse: the spread of the gospel can be compromised too. Upstream Work for Managers As a manager, if you notice someone isn’t performing well, the best time to start talking about it isn’t at the exit conversation. It’s way upstream from that. Your core job is to ensure your people have what they need to be successful. That includes clear expectations, communication of what success looks like, feedback on performance, and accountability for meeting those standards. Ideally, you’re doing these on a regular basis in one-on-one meetings  and in performance check-ins throughout the year. Churches and nonprofits must hire capable people who can effectively perform their duties and steward the mission. This is a manager’s job, and faith-based organizations don’t have a softer standard. Where I’ve seen termination decisions and conversations go south—in Christian organizations or elsewhere—is when a manager doesn’t understand this. (Or, worse, they understand it but think that somehow it doesn’t apply to them.) Speaking to an employee about parting ways because you’ve consistently documented underperformance is a rough conversation. It’s far worse when your failure to give regular feedback leaves an employee blindsided, confused, and hurt when you need to broach termination. Often, that failure is rooted in a desire to avoid conflict or hurt feelings. The manager would rather spare himself the discomfort of a direct conversation. In a Christian organization, this impulse pulls hard. The employees under your care all love Jesus. They’re there to promote the church’s mission and spread the gospel. You may even sit shoulder to shoulder in the pews with them on Sundays. But James 4:17 has a word for managers who fail to do the difficult work: “Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.” Colossians 4:1 underlines this: “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.” I’ve watched managers avoid the perceived sin of commission (telling someone he’s doing a poor job in his role) and step right into the sin of omission (letting the problem fester until the employee is struggling and a termination conversation seems inevit

featured.title: The Festive Attire We Really Need
featured.summary: Even in our finest clothes we can still be dirty on the inside. Advent reminds us that Jesus dresses us in his righteousness.
featured.summary_zh: 即使穿着我们最好的衣服 内心还是可以脏的 基督提醒我们,耶稣穿戴我们的正义。
featured.title_zh: 我们真正需要的节奏
featured.content: Read He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD. Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD as in the days of old and as in former years. (Mal. 3:3–4) Reflect My grandmother always made going to church a special event. She helped me pick the right dress, made sure my shoes were shiny and clean, and withstood burns from the curling iron to perfect my hairdo. I know church attire can vary. But I still get dressed up for corporate worship because, no matter how cliché it sounds, I want to wear my Sunday best for Jesus. Yet even in our finest clothes, we can still be dirty on the inside. Hidden sins are, after all, hidden. We can sing hymns at max volume, forgetting the way we treated our coworkers last week. We can kneel in prayer, easily dismissing what we posted on the internet earlier that morning. We can take the bread and wine even if we lost it with our kids in the car. People at church only see what’s on the outside, but God looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). And unless we come clean, we can’t come into his presence at all. Even in our finest clothes, we can still be dirty on the inside. Purity in God’s presence is a major theme in Scripture. In Leviticus, we learn how Israel was to distinguish between the clean and unclean. These categories extended to foods and animals. Even people could be defiled by disease or by touching unclean things such as a dead body. The temple was off-limits for the unclean. Only ritual washings and animal sacrifices made reentry into God’s presence achievable. But even this wasn’t permanent—for the blood of bulls and goats couldn’t fully atone for sin (Heb. 10:4). Like Israel, we dare not present ourselves before God in our sinful condition. As the psalmist asks, “Who shall stand in [God’s] holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Ps. 24:3–4). While soap and water might wash our filthy hands, what can purify our sin-stained hearts? In today’s verses, the prophet Malachi announced the coming of One who would refine his people as gold and silver. Later, the author of Hebrews clarified the refiner’s identity: If the blood of goats and bulls . . . sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God. (Heb. 9:13–14) During Advent, we remember that Jesus is the great Refiner. He came to shed his purifying blood to cover our sins and forgive us. Then, like a refiner who heats metal to remove impurities, the Lord sanctifies us so that on judgment day we’ll be an unblemished offering to God. On that day, because of Jesus, we’ll wear white robes of righteousness (Rev. 6:11). Grandma made sure I looked pretty for church, but I wasn’t truly clean. Jesus, the great Purifier of sinners, is the only One who can wash away every stain and remove every impurity. When he dresses us in white robes, we’ll enter God’s presence because we’ll be clean—not just on the outside but on the inside too. Respond Sometimes the Lord refines us through trials and difficult circumstances. How have you experienced his refining process this year? Write a prayer thanking God for Christ who cleanses, purifies, and refines us so we’ll one day be holy and acceptable in his presence.

她帮我选合适的裙子 确保我的鞋子光亮洁洁 从卷曲的铁里烧伤 我知道教堂的服装会有所不同 但我还是穿好衣服去参加公司礼拜 因为不管这听起来多么陈词滥调 我想穿我的星期天最好的耶稣。 即便穿着我们最好的衣服 我们内心仍然可以肮脏

隐藏的罪恶毕竟是隐藏的。 我们可以用最高音量唱颂歌 忘记上周我们对待同事的方式 我们可以跪在祷告中, 轻易地放弃我们当天早晨在互联网上发布的内容。 我们可以拿走面包和酒 即使我们失去了它与我们的孩子在车里。 人们在教堂只看到外面的东西,但上帝看着心脏(1Sam. 16:7).

除非我们坦白,否则我们根本无法进入他的存在。 即使穿着我们最好的衣服, 我们内部仍然可以脏。 上帝面前的纯洁是圣经中的一个主要主题。 在利维提库斯,我们了解到以色列如何区分干净和不干净。 这些类别扩大到食物和动物。

甚至人们也可能因疾病或触摸尸体等不干净的东西而受到玷污。 该寺对不洁者禁入. 只有仪式洗涤和动物牺牲才能使重返上帝的存在。 但即使是这也不是永久的 — — 因为公牛和山羊的血无法完全赎罪(Heb. 10:4)。

与以色列一样,我们不敢在罪恶的条件下站在上帝面前。 正如诗人所问的, " 谁会站在[上帝]的圣地? 手清净而心清净者”(第24:3-4页)。 虽然肥皂和水可能洗我们的脏手,但什么能净化我们的罪恶的心? 先知马拉奇在今天的诗文中宣布,

后来,希伯来人的作者澄清了提炼者的身份: 如果山羊和公牛的血... ...为净化肉体而神圣化, 基督的血会有多少, 他通过永恒的灵献给自己 没有污垢上帝, (Heb. 9:13-14)在"启示录"中,我们记得耶稣是伟大的炼油者.

他为了掩盖我们的罪孽 并原谅我们而来 然后,像精炼者一样,他用金属加热去除杂质,主使我们圣洁,这样,在审判日,我们将成为向上帝献礼的无瑕疵者。 因为耶稣的缘故, 外婆确保我看起来很适合教堂,

耶稣,罪人的伟大净化者,是唯一可以洗去每一个污点,去除每一个杂质的人. 当他穿白袍时, 我们将进入上帝的面前, 有时主会通过考验和困难的环境来完善我们 你今年是怎么经历他的提炼过程的?

感谢上帝净化、净化、精炼我们,

featured.summary_zh: 六个帖子中的第四个帖子包含了阿尔伯特· N ·马丁（ Albert N. Martin ）在1984年旗帜青年大会（ Banner Youth Conference ）上给出的教学内容，展示了基督教生活的基本圣经神学。在基督徒的生活中，没有承诺或命令的危机经历是必不可少的元素。一些关于基督徒生活的教导断言， […]《基督徒生活中没有必要的危机经历》一文首先出现在《美国真理旗帜》上。
featured.title_zh: 在基督徒的生活中，没有必要的危机经历
featured.content: The fourth of six posts containing the substance of teaching given by Albert N. Martin at the 1984 Banner Youth Conference, presenting a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. There is no crisis experience promised or commanded as an essential element in living the Christian life. Some teaching on the Christian life asserts that only a low level of Christian experience can be realized by the person who has not had a crisis experience subsequent to regeneration, or at least subsequent to conversion and to the beginning of conscious Christian experience. Furthermore, it is asserted that the crisis experience is both commanded and promised by God as the entrance into a qualitatively new dimension or level of spiritual experience, reality and power. Throughout the history of the Christian church there have been many different strands of this crisis teaching. There is what we might call ‘classic Wesleyan perfectionism,’ which concentrated particularly upon sanctification and spoke of a baptism of purifying fire, or of coming into a state of perfect love. It concentrated not so much on power for service or upon inward feelings, but on a crisis experience in which the power of indwelling sin was to all intents and purposes negated. I have read enough of classic Wesleyan theology to know that there are different opinions as to what John Wesley himself taught on the subject. But in a general descriptive manner this, I believe, is an accurate representation of old-style classic Wesleyan perfectionism. Then, too, there is ‘the old Pentecostalism’ in which the emphasis was upon a baptism in the Holy Spirit, generally subsequent to conversion, and invariably manifested by speaking in tongues: the way you knew that you had this baptism of power was that, when it came to you, you spoke in tongues. The primary focus in old classic Pentecostalism was the matter of power for service. Thirdly, there is the modern ‘charismatic movement.’ Like classic Pentecostalism, its teachers use many of the same passages in the Book of Acts to support their theory of this necessary crisis. So they emphasize that in most cases—although there are different schools among modern charismatics—it will be manifested by the speaking in tongues. Some are content to believe you have ‘got it’ if you have a season of holy laughter. Others, however, say that you have not spoken in tongues because you have some psychological hold-ups, and if these can be removed the tongues are there. You just have not given them utterance. Here the emphasis is not so much on a baptism of purifying fire (as in the case of old classic Wesleyan perfectionism), or the baptism of power (as in the case of old classic Pentecostalism), but more upon a baptism of joyful praise-filled experience. I have been speaking of generalities, but I believe they are accurate. Fourthly, there are the various forms of ‘higher life’ teaching. What they have in common is this: you are simply converted, simply united to Christ, simply regenerated, and then you come to a crisis of surrender and faith, in which ‘you let go and let God’ and appropriate the indwelling life of Christ. The common denominator is that it is a crisis without any external manifestation of tongues or holy laughter or shouting or jumping, but the end result will be new power to live a holy life—the emphasis falls upon the ability to be more efficient in the path of holiness. Fifthly, there is a kind of teaching which has both old and modern proponents. It focuses on assurance, and has been expressed in terms of the biblical language of a ‘sealing of the Holy Spirit.’ Some of the Puritans—Thomas Goodwin, for example—taught this. There have been certain preachers in our own day who have believed this very strongly and emphasized it repeatedly. The basic concern in this teaching is that, subsequent to regeneration and conversion, there is a crisis experience in which the believer enters into a qualitatively new dimension of assurance by
featured.content_zh: 阿尔伯特·N·马丁在1984年班纳青年会议上发表的包含教学内容的六篇文章中的第四篇,介绍了基督教生活的基本圣经神学. 没有任何危机经历作为过上基督教生活的一项基本要素得到承诺或接受。 一些关于基督教生活的教义主张,在再生后,或至少是在皈依后,以及自觉的基督教经历开始后,没有危机经历的人,只有低水平的基督教经验才能实现. 此外,有人断言,危机经历既是上帝的旨意,也是上帝的允诺,是精神经历、现实和力量进入一个全新的层面或层次的。 在基督教会的历史上,这种危机教育有许多不同的内容。 我们可能称之为“经典的卫斯理完美主义 ” , 它不是把精力集中在服务或内在感情上,而是集中在一种危机经历上,在这种经历中,罪恶的威力是所有意图和目的所否定的。 我读了足够多的经典的卫斯理神学,知道对于约翰·卫斯理自己教授的这个主题,有不同的看法. 但从一般的描述方式来看,我认为,这是对老式经典的卫斯理主义的准确表述. 也存在“五旬节派”的旧现象, 重点是圣灵中的洗礼, 通常是在皈依之后, 古老的经典五旬节主义的主要焦点是服务的权力问题. 第三,有现代`魅力运动'。 和经典的五旬节主义一样,它的老师们也用"行动书"中的许多同名段落来支持他们对这个必要危机的理论. 所以他们强调,在多数情况下,尽管现代魅力中存在着不同的学校,但用舌头说话将表明这一点。 如果你有一个圣笑的季节, 然而,其他人说,你没有说出舌头,因为你有一些心理障碍,如果这些障碍可以取出,舌头就在那里。 你只是没说 这里强调的不是净化火的洗礼(如旧经典的卫斯理完美主义),也不是权力的洗礼(如旧经典的五旬节主义),而是更强调充满欢乐的赞美经验的洗礼. 我一直在谈论泛泛而谈,但我认为它们是正确的。 第四,有各种形式的 " 更高的生活 " 教学。 他们的共同点是:你们只是皈依正教,只是与基督联合,只是再生,然后你们遭遇了投降和信仰的危机,你们在危机中“放手,放任真主出征”,而顺从基督永生。 共同的分母是,这是一场没有外在表现出舌头或圣笑或叫喊或跳跃的危机,但最终结果将是新的力量来过上圣生活——强调在圣道上更有效率的能力. 第五,有一种教学既有老的也有现代的支持者。 它侧重于保证,并用圣经中的"封圣"来表述. 一些清教徒——例如托马斯·古德温——教授了这个。 在我们这一天里,有一些传道者非常强烈地相信并反复强调这一点。 该教学的基本关注是,在再生和转生之后,存在着一种危机经历,信仰者通过下列方式进入了保证的质的新层面:

featured.content: Audio Transcript We lived through a decade of smartphone abuse and overuse (roughly 2015 to 2024). We talked at length about it on this podcast. I wrote books about it. Most of us have come to terms with when and where we’ve been online too much. We lament the wasted time, knowing we should have been doing more important things. The clock sped up as we lost ourselves in the everlasting scroll of eye-grabbing images and video. But what if time was not the greatest cost? What if something more serious happened to us, a lingering damage still present inside of us now? Today on Ask Pastor John: scrolling the soul shallow. It’s a question from Noah, a young man in Akron, Ohio. “Pastor John, I have made Titus 2:6–8 my aim as a young man. I know Paul is speaking to a young pastor. I am not a pastor, but I want to be self-controlled. I want to show myself ‘to be a model of good works,’ and I want to display ‘integrity, dignity, and sound speech.’ The main struggle I face is the shallowness of the culture in which we live. On my phone, computer, and TV, I see endless examples of flippancy. That’s really all I see some days. The whole world seems bent on numbing our souls to eternal realities. How can a young man resist all this and stay spiritually alert and cultivate these virtues?” One of the reasons I love this question is because I have said many times that the worst problem with television (or now let’s just say Instagram or any online media in general) is probably not the pervasive sexualization of all of life — that’s big enough — but rather the pervasive trivialization of all of life. You can scarcely watch TV ads or be online for more than ten seconds without being dump-trucked with banality and silliness. Grown men and women, even famous grown men and women, act like eleven-year-olds whose high point at summer camp was to bob for apples in a toilet filled with Mello Yello — the apex of satisfaction. That’s the quality that we’re being dumped on every day. This is the world we live in: silliness, humor, fun, joking, casual, flippant, cleverness, whimsical. And all that has made its way tragically into parenting, worship services, preaching, and hosting an event, even a serious one. Many modern people have never tasted serious joy, glad gravity, happy earnestness, or joyful weightiness. They have no category for such a thing. There’s fun and there’s boredom. That’s it. Life is that shallow, that insignificant. So, Noah asks, “How can I resist all this? How can I march to the beat of a different drummer?” 1. Distinguish between joy and fun. First, make sure that you are clear that joy and fun are not identical. Today, the word fun has virtually taken over the experience of serious joy. “Think about the shortness of life and the inevitability of death and the great realities of God.” Fun is what you have when playing with your kids on the living-room floor, flag football with the guys on Saturday, or a day at Disney World. That’s fun — nothing wrong with it. But now, church planting is fun, worship services are fun, Bible studies are fun. It’s as if you learn the language of trees while walking among twenty-foot Georgia pines, and then you visit three-hundred-foot, two-thousand-year-old redwoods in California and you have no language. They’re just fun trees. They’re not magnificent. They’re not breathtaking. They’re not humbling. They’re just fun trees. So, Noah, grow your vocabulary of joy and significance and wonder, because more often than we would like to admit, the heart shrinks to the language we have to express it rather than the other way around. If you call enough magnificent things “fun,” before long, that’s all they’ll be. Your heart will have shrunk to your vocabulary. 2. Know you’re not crazy. Second, listen to the warnings of Scripture to know you’re not crazy. The Bible is very aware of people who are incapable of being happily serious, and all their language is just clever or joking or trifling. - “Like a madman w

音频记录 我们经历了十年的智能手机虐待和过度使用(大约2015年到2024年). 我们在播客上详细谈论了这个问题。 我写过书 我们大部分人都同意我们上网的时间和地点。 我们对浪费时间感到遗憾,因为我们知道我们应该做更重要的事。

时钟加速了,因为我们迷失了自己 在永恒的卷轴 挖眼影像和视频。 但如果时间不是最大的代价呢? 如果更严重的事情发生在我们身上, 那现在我们体内仍然存在的伤害呢? 今天在"问约翰牧师"上:滚动灵魂浅浅. 俄亥俄州Akron的年轻人Noah问:

“约翰神父,我把提图斯2:6-8作为我作为年轻人的目标。 我知道保罗在和一个年轻的牧师说话 我不是牧师,但我想自我控制。 我想展示自己“成为优秀作品的典范”, 我面临的主要斗争是我们所生活的文化的浅浅.

在我的手机、电脑和电视上, 我看到无尽的翻转例子。 这些日子我只看到这些。 整个世界似乎都想把我们的灵魂麻木于永恒的现实。

一个年轻人怎么能抗拒这一切,保持精神警惕,培养这些美德呢?” 我喜欢这个问题的原因之一 是因为我已经说过很多次了 电视最糟糕的问题(或者现在我们只说Instagram或任何一般的网络媒体) 可能不是 普遍的性化 生活的所有 - 这已经够大了 - 而是 普遍的轻视所有o

f 寿. 你几乎不能看电视广告 或在线超过十秒 而不被垃圾车 与平庸和愚蠢。 长大的男女,甚至著名的成年男女,都表现得像11岁的孩子,他们在夏令营的高潮是在充满了梅洛·耶洛的厕所里为苹果吹嘘——满足的顶峰. 这就是我们每天被抛弃的质量。

这就是我们生活的世界: 愚蠢、幽默、有趣、开玩笑、随意、放荡、聪明、狂喜。 在养育子女、礼拜、传教和主持活动,甚至是严肃的活动方面,所有这一切都是可悲的。 许多现代人从未品尝过严肃的喜悦,快乐的引力,快乐的真诚,或者欢乐的重量. 他们没有这样的分类。

有乐趣和无聊。 就这样。 生命是那么浅,那么微不足道。 诺亚问道:我怎能抗拒这一切呢? 我怎能走向一个不同的鼓手呢?” 1.区分欢喜乐. 第一,确保你明白快乐和乐趣并不相同。 今天,乐趣一词几乎取代了严肃的欢乐经历.

“考虑到生命的短暂性、死亡的必然性和上帝的伟大现实。” 有趣的是,当你在客厅地板上和孩子们玩时, 星期六和男生一起打橄榄球, 或者一天在迪士尼世界。 这很有趣, 但现在,教堂的栽培是乐趣,礼拜服务是乐趣,圣经研究是乐趣.

就像在二十英尺高的乔治亚松林中学习树木语言, 他们只是有趣的树。 他们并不伟大。 他们并不令人惊叹。 他们不会发抖。 他们只是有趣的树。

所以,诺亚, 增加你的喜悦和意义 和奇异的词汇, 因为比我们想承认的更多时候, 心脏收缩到 语言 我们必须表达它而不是相反。 如果你在不久之前就称它为“有趣”的话, 你的心会缩到词汇里 2. 知道你没有疯。

第二,听从圣经的警告, 圣经中非常了解那些不能快乐严肃的人,他们所有的语言都只是聪明或开玩笑,或三思而行. - 像个疯子

featured.content: Tuesday is the day most publishers release their new books, so each week I like to let you know what has just come our way from the publishers I follow most closely. It is a quieter week than the last one, but it brings a revised edition of B. B. Warfield’s Biblical and Theological Studies, Alex Duke’s guided tour of Exodus (for which I provided a foreword), and two Crossway editions marking 500 years since William Tyndale’s English New Testament. On the academic side, you’ll find several noteworthy titles, including the New International Commentary on the Old Testament volume on Daniel 7–12. In each case, I’ve included the publisher’s description. Books for Everyone Zondervan From Silence to Sinai A Guided Tour of Exodus Alex Duke Publisher’s description What adjectives would you use to describe the Bible? Inspired. Amazing. Unique. Authoritative. Perfect. Pure. Life-changing. Those descriptions are all deserved. Your pastors and parents and Sunday School teachers were right. There’s no book like God’s Book. Here’s another adjective: confusing. The Bible can be confusing, especially certain parts of the Old Testament. Moments after coming across something inspiring and encouraging, you’ll read something that makes you wonder, What is even happening right now!? The book of Exodus is no exception. This sequel to Genesis begins with God’s surprising silence. What a stark contrast to Genesis, where God’s words set everything in motion. It then tells the story of God’s miraculous liberation of his people, complete with frogs falling from the sky and life-saving blood being painted over doorways. Finally, for the last half of the book, the action slows down as the people of God gather at the mountain of God to receive the Law of God in order to engage in the worship of God. From silence to Sinai, that’s the story of Exodus. To understand it all, most of us will need a guide. We’ll need some help. That’s what From Silence to Sinai is for. Alex Duke walks readers through the book of Exodus to show that nothing in God’s story is wasted—not the silence, not the ten signs, and not even the confusing parts. featured.title_zh: 您就不能做点新东西吗？
featured.content: How often does church-leadership content online reveal a lightly veiled obsession with new ? The experts today might not come out and say it, but the assumption often seems to be: Surely after two thousand years and all of our light-year advances in technology, the church needs a serious upgrade. Capturing this sentiment, one article insists, “Church leaders face two options. Either battle the marketplace currents and strive to convince enough people to pay for sermon-centric Sunday gatherings, or rethink that model to better fit the realities of making disciples in the twenty-first century.” Someone recently shared a clip with me that illustrates one such updated model. The video features a popular preacher who begins his Sunday sermon by driving a Rolls-Royce onto a stage. Twenty-two screens surround him, and hundreds of light bulbs hang overhead. The “preacher” steps out of the half-a-million-dollar car and takes critics like me head-on: There are some of you who are saying, “Oh man, I can’t believe you drove a Rolls-Royce into church. Man, that’s gimmicky.” No, it’s not; it’s godly. “Oh, that’s trite. That’s flippant.” No, it’s from Christ’s playbook. If you ever go to church and you find yourself bored, blame the communicator, the pastor. Don’t blame God. Yeah, for some reason we go to church and expect boredom. Just the opposite should be true. We are — and this is going to mess you up — we are in the entertainment business. I agree that no one should be bored in church — and I certainly agree that God is not to blame for any boredom in the pews. This preacher’s gimmick implies, however, that the same old formula for church — prayer, singing, fellowship, preaching — can’t possibly keep the attention of modern people like you. Mere sermons won’t cut it. God needs us to spice things up. God is not surprised by our state-of-the-art technology or shriveling attention spans, and he has told us, from the beginning, what captures souls when we gather for worship. He’s told us how to do church, and his counsel hasn’t expired. A Church Anyone Would Want Do you want to hear about a church that was emphatically not bored? They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. And awe came upon every soul , and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common. And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved. (Acts 2:42–47) Don’t you want to be a part of a church like that? Don’t you want your local church to taste the camaraderie, sacrifice, growth, and joy these people experienced when they gathered? The God-authored recipe is remarkably simple and durable: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” What did this church do when it grew so wildly and unexpectedly? They gathered. They ate. They gave. They prayed. They preached. And because they devoted themselves to God’s inspired Sunday-service plan, they rejoiced and their numbers multiplied. It’s dumbfounding that we see this kind of church thrive for literally millennia and still conclude it’s time to shake things up. “Sunday sermons got us this far,” we say, “but we’ll take it from here.” What if God knew everything we know — artificial intelligence, fiber-optic internet, driverless cars, those new robot vacuums that can clean stairs — and deliberately told churches to pray, sing, eat, drink, and preach the word anyway? Preaching to Itching Ears God knew exactly what changes and pressures our churches would face in the twenty-first century, and so he warned us t

featured.content: The world has a lot to say to the next generation about identity and sexuality.
